procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 9, 1967, of the Patna High Court in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 31 of 1967, dismissing the appellant's application for a writ of habeas corpus.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant, Rameshwar Lal Patwari, filed a writ petition (under Art. 226 of the Constitution and s. 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure) in the Patna High Court seeking a writ of habeas corpus for his release from detention. The High Court scrutinized the grounds of detention and dismissed his petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's conclusion that his complaint had no substance. He argued that some of the grounds for his detention did not exist in fact, while others were vague or irrelevant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court can scrutinize the material on which the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is based, even if it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds.

facts: An appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on grounds of alleged black-marketing.
The grounds supplied to the appellant were challenged as being vague, non-existent, or false.
Specifically, one ground referred to a pending case against the appellant, but he had already been tried and acquitted in that case months earlier.
The High Court dismissed the appellant's writ petition, leading to an appeal to the Supreme Court.
law: The formation of an opinion for preventive detention is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
Courts are not an appellate authority and cannot rule on the sufficiency or reasonableness of the grounds for detention.
However, because detention without trial is a serious matter, the court must perform the "closest scrutiny of the material on which the decision is formed" to check for errors.
The grounds supplied to the detenu must not be vague, indefinite, or non-existent, as this would deny the detenu a real opportunity to make a representation.

If a vital ground is shown to be non-existent, false, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated, as it is impossible to know how much that faulty ground contributed to the authority's subjective satisfaction.
application: The Court first reiterated the principle that it cannot substitute its own objective judgment for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority regarding the sufficiency of the grounds.
However, it asserted its duty to scrutinize the material itself. The Court found that the detention order in this case was based on several grounds, some of which were vague.

Crucially, one ground was found to be false or non-existent: the detaining authority was unaware that the appellant had been acquitted in a case it cited as a reason for detention. The Court called this a display of carelessness and a lack of due care.

Applying the established law, the Court reasoned that since some of the grounds were non-existent or vague, the entire detention order was invalid. It refused to speculate whether the remaining grounds would have been sufficient on their own, as that would mean substituting a judicial test for the authority's subjective one.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that while it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds for detention, it can and must scrutinize the material on which the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction is based. If any of the grounds are found to be vague, non-existent, or false, the entire detention order is vitiated because it's impossible to determine the extent to which the invalid ground influenced the authority's decision. The detention was therefore held to be illegal.

issue.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be sustained if one of the grounds supplied is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant.

facts: An appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on grounds of alleged black-marketing.
The appellant challenged the detention, arguing that the grounds supplied to him were vague or non-existent.
Upon review, the Court found that at least two grounds were vague, and one was false, as it referred to a pending case in which the appellant had already been tried and acquitted months earlier.
law: The court cannot assess the sufficiency or reasonableness of the grounds for detention, as this is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
However, if one of several grounds provided for detention is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated (invalidated).
The court cannot separate the valid grounds from the invalid ones and uphold the order on the basis of the remaining grounds.

This is because it is impossible for a court to determine how each individual ground influenced the mind of the detaining authority and contributed to their subjective satisfaction. To do so would be to substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive, which is against the policy of the statute.
application: In this case, the Court identified several defective grounds, including some that were vague and one that was factually false (non-existent).
The Court noted that referring to an acquitted case as a pending one showed a serious lack of care and attention by the detaining authority.
Applying the established legal principle, the Court refused to speculate on whether the remaining grounds would have been sufficient to justify the detention.

Because some of the grounds were non-existent and vague, the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority was considered to be based on flawed material, thus invalidating the entire detention order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a detention order could be sustained if one of its grounds was non-existent, vague, or irrelevant. The Court held that if any single ground is found to be defective, the entire order is invalid because it is impossible to know to what extent the faulty ground influenced the subjective decision of the detaining authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention supplied to the appellant were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, or based on carelessness.

facts: The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on the grounds that he was engaged in the black-marketing of food grains.
The grounds of detention supplied to him included several specific allegations.
The Supreme Court examined these grounds and found significant flaws.
One ground referred to a pending criminal case against the appellant, but he had actually been tried and acquitted in that case months before the detention order was issued.

Another ground, alleging the purchase and smuggling of food grains, was deemed vague because it lacked essential details like the names of shops or dates of purchase, making it impossible for the appellant to effectively counter the allegation.
Other grounds were also found to be deficient or based on a "lame excuse".
law: While a court cannot question the sufficiency or reasonableness of the grounds for detention (as this is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority), it can scrutinize the material on which the decision is based.
The grounds provided to a detainee must not be vague or indefinite; they must be precise and detailed enough to allow the person to make an effective representation against their detention.
If some of the grounds are found to be non-existent, false, or are later given up, the entire detention order is vitiated and cannot be justified.

The court cannot separate the valid grounds from the invalid ones to see if the valid ones would be sufficient to sustain the order, as this would substitute the court's objective judgment for the executive's subjective satisfaction.
application: The Court applied the legal principles to the facts and found that the grounds for detention in this case had two major defects.

First, some grounds were non-existent or false. The reference to a "pending case" in which the appellant had already been acquitted was a clear factual error, which the Court described as displaying "carelessness which is extremely disturbing" and a "disregard for truth and accuracy."
Second, other grounds were too vague to allow for an effective representation. The allegation of smuggling lacked the necessary particulars for the appellant to refute it.
Because at least one ground was false and others were vague, the Court concluded that the entire detention order was invalid, in line with its previous rulings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, holding that the detention was illegal because the grounds supplied were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, and based on carelessness. The Court allowed the appeal and ordered the appellant's immediate release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court can scrutinize the material on which the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is based, even if it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the court has the power and duty to scrutinize the grounds of detention to determine if they are existent, relevant, and not vague.
The appellant challenged the grounds in the High Court and the Supreme Court, claiming some did not exist in fact, while others were vague or irrelevant, thereby inviting judicial scrutiny.
respondent_arguments: The respondent, defending the High Court's decision, implicitly argued that while the court could scrutinize the grounds, the High Court had already done so and correctly found the appellant's complaint had no substance.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be sustained if one of the grounds supplied is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's entire case was premised on the argument that because several grounds were non-existent, vague, or false, the entire detention order was illegal and could not be sustained.
respondent_arguments: The respondent attempted to defend each ground individually, arguing for instance that even though the appellant was acquitted on one ground, the facts still existed and he was not handicapped in making a representation. This implies an argument that the detention order could be sustained even if some grounds were challenged.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention supplied to the appellant were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, or based on carelessness.
appellant_arguments: The grounds were non-existent, vague, or otherwise deficient.
One ground was based on a case in which the appellant had already been acquitted, rendering it false.
A ground alleging the purchase of paddy in 'fictitious names' was too vague to be effectively challenged, as it lacked details like shop names or dates.
Another ground was based solely on a driver's statement without any proper inquiry, showing a jump to conclusions.
respondent_arguments: The grounds were not non-existent; the facts of the case where the appellant was acquitted still existed even after the acquittal.
The appellant had full knowledge of the facts of the case he was acquitted in and was therefore not handicapped in making a representation.
The respondent's counsel conceded that some details were necessary for the ground concerning purchases in 'fictitious names'.

cases.principle: If one of several grounds for a detention order is found to be invalid, illusory, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated. The court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority to determine if the remaining grounds are sufficient.

cases.case_name: Keshav Talpade v. The King Emperor
cases.principle: If one of several grounds for a detention order is found to be invalid, illusory, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated. The court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority to determine if the remaining grounds are sufficient.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If a preventive detention order is based on multiple grounds, and one of those grounds is found to be non-existent, irrelevant, or illusory, the entire detention order is vitiated as a whole, because a court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority to determine if the remaining grounds would have been sufficient.
obiter: The sufficiency of the grounds for a detention order cannot be agitated before a court, as courts are not an appellate authority over the subjective satisfaction of the detaining officer.
The detention of a person without trial requires the closest scrutiny of the material on which the decision is formed.
The grounds for detention must not be vague or indefinite and must afford a real opportunity for the detenu to make a representation against the detention.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found the detention illegal because the grounds supplied to the appellant were defective. Specifically, at least two grounds were vague, one was false (as it related to a case where the appellant had been acquitted), and another was based on a jump to a conclusion without proper inquiry. Citing established legal principles, the court held that where some grounds are found to be non-existent or are otherwise invalid, the entire detention order is vitiated and cannot be justified, as it is impossible for the court to determine to what extent the invalid grounds contributed to the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
legal_tests_applied: If one of several grounds for a detention order is found to be non-existent, irrelevant, or illusory, the entire detention order is vitiated. The court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority by assessing whether the remaining grounds are sufficient to sustain the order.
The grounds of detention must be sufficiently precise and furnish enough details to enable the person detained to make an effective representation; if they do not, the detention can be questioned.
policy_considerations: Powers of detention without a trial, which should be exercised with the greatest care and attention, had been exercised in this case with such disregard for truth and accuracy.

For a detaining authority to be unaware that a person had been tried and acquitted months before, and to still consider the pendency of that case as a ground for detention, shows that due care and attention is not being paid to such serious matters as detention without trial.
